en: The Drona Parva (The Book of the Fall of Droṇa)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
Hearing that Suravrata had been slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was exceedingly distressed; again and again he lamented for that subduer of enemies, who was a mass of glory.
Then, having witnessed the battle once more, Saṃjaya returned;
questioned by the son of Vicitravīrya, he described the slaughter of the heroes.
Then, O King, when Bhīṣma had been slain, the Kurus were deeply distressed,
like merchants who have fallen into the ocean after their ship has been wrecked.
They beheld Karṇa arrived at the battle, their longed-for refuge,
like those sold in foreign lands who see a loving kinsman in times of distress.
Then Duryodhana, an ocean of fortitude, suppressing his grief with the consent of Karṇa, appointed Droṇa as the leader of the armies.
Having been duly consecrated by him as the preceptor of all archers,
that powerful hero shone like a second Mahāsena.
The white umbrella of his own glory shone over the aged king,
like the radiant orb of the moon rising from the ocean of milk.
Clad in golden armor, he shone with radiant rays,
like one attended by divine weapons that have arrived at the time for action.
The leader of all heroes, equal in abundant splendor,
he was like the science of archery personified— the very limit of the scriptures for destruction.
He departed in a golden chariot drawn by crimson horses and adorned with banners,
like the sun setting behind Mount Meru with its twilight-hued, cascading streams.
Upon his chariot shone a golden water-pot,
like his own majesty condensed into a single mass by the heat of his valor.
With grey hair reaching his ears, dark-complexioned, the leader of all archers,
and endowed with splendor, he granted a boon when requested by the king himself.
"Taking King Yudhiṣṭhira alive, I shall deliver him to Arjuna when he has been slain, while all the kings look on. (Bhājana 7.14)
Having received these words of his preceptor with palms joined in reverence,
the king caused them to be proclaimed among his own troops and celebrated with the festive sounding of trumpets.
And the son of Dharma, having learned of this together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
formed the Krauñca array and, fully armored, set out to fight.
When Droṇa had formed the extremely compact cart-array (śakaṭavyūha),
a great battle took place among the heroes, one that shattered their bodies.
Then, upon the armies of the Sṛñjayas, Pāñcālas, and Matsyas,
there fell irresistible arrows marked with Droṇa’s name, which carried away their bodies.
While the armies were being shattered, with elephants and horses falling, and even the chariots swept away by the currents of rivers of blood; Bhmj_7.19 //
Droṇa’s son, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and others, highly incensed, held back the heroes headed by Yudhiṣṭhira who were rushing toward Droṇa in a fit of rage.
Then Abhimanyu, having dragged the Paurava from his chariot by the hair,
struck him down with a sword while all the archers looked on.
In his anger, the hero took up his sword and rendered Jayadratha— who had approached him—
and Śalya, the best among the strong, both deprived of their chariots.
Then Śalya, mace in hand, rushed at the son of Subhadrā on foot;
Bhīma, with his heroic-slaying mace, held him back.
Between the two of them, a terrible club-duel ensued, which bewildered men and was filled with sparks from their mutual blows.
Moving in circles like two elephants in rut,
they rushed at each other and struck one another with their maces after eight steps.
Seeing those two fallen, their minds overwhelmed by a fainting spell born of deep wounds, the heroic strikers gathered together.
Once the lord of the Madras had been swiftly led away by Kṛtavarman on his chariot,
Bhīmasena seized the Kuru army and tore it asunder.
Then, seeing the sons of Draupadī covered by the arrows of Dṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, the Pāṇḍavas rushed toward him.
Then Droṇa, on his golden chariot, having himself entered the Pāñcāla army,
scattered it in a thousand directions with his arrows.
Having pierced through the great chariot-warriors headed by Śikhaṇḍin and Sātyaki,
he gazed toward Yudhiṣṭhira while causing the destruction of kings.
With arrows as terrible as thunderbolts, he sent Yugaṃdhara, Vyāghradatta, and King Siṃhasena to the abode of Death.
"Stay! I am standing; fight! You are slain!"—thus did the battle proceed among the kings fighting before Droṇa, as they cried out again and again.
Hearing the clamor of his own troops as they fought with Droṇa, Śvetavāhana quickly arrived at that place. (Bhājana 7.33)
Having struck down the Kuru army with a net of missiles, that hero created a river of blood, from which elephants were swept away by the whirlpools.
Then, afflicted by the arrows of Pārtha,
those bulls among the Kurus withdrew their armies when the sun of fierce rays had set.
***** The Consecration of Droṇa and the First Day of Battle ***** When all the kings had settled in their camps during the night,
the Teacher, as if feeling ashamed, spoke to Duryodhana: (Bhājana 7.36)
"I have already said this, O King: I shall capture Yudhiṣṭhira when he is deprived of Savyasācin; for Dhanañjaya is indeed difficult to conquer."
While the teacher was speaking thus out of embarrassment in the presence of the king,
the King of Tri-garta, who had harbored enmity toward Arjuna, spoke.
We were [surrounded] by hosts of Saṃśaptakas, as well as by the Tuṇḍilas,
and by heroic Madrakas, Kāmbojas, and graceful strikers.
Having summoned Pārtha with thirty thousand chariots and stationed themselves separately, they said, "We shall fight with our well-prepared forces; we swear this as the truth."
When this was said, the Trigarta heroes, with King Suśarman at their head, took an oath with fire as their witness and set forth at dawn.
With the surface of the sky swallowed by the dust raised by the hooves of their horses,
they issued cries foreboding universal destruction as they called out for Phalguna.
Seeing them stationed on level ground in the crescent formation,
Pārtha, having been challenged, then addressed Yudhiṣṭhira.
"May the Noble One grant me permission for the slaughter of the Trigartas;
these men, full of rivalry, desire to fight with me."
This Satyajit, the hero of the Pañcālas, is your preeminent chariot-warrior;
equal to Śakra in prowess, he is the protector in the encounter with Droṇa.
Having spoken thus, he whose banner is the monkey, making the quarters of the sky resound with the fierce roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
advanced toward them like the turbulent ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
Seeing the son of Pāṇḍu approaching, they too, filled with intense joy,
quickly made him invisible with their arrows, like a blossoming *sāla* tree.
Then Dhananjaya blew his conch shell— the foam of the ocean of heroism, the loud laughter of the goddess of battle, and the bulbous root of the tree of his own fame.
At that great and terrifying sound, his army stood still,
with its elephants halted and its limbs and horses motionless.
Then, with a net of arrows that snatched away the living fish,
Pārtha surrounded the Trigarta army on all sides.
Then, as the expanse of the world was covered by the arrow-holes released by the hosts of Saṃśaptakas, an unseasonable night fell.
Then the son of the wielder of the thunderbolt discharged the great Tvaṣṭra-weapon,
by which those [enemies], filled with agitation, beheld thousands of Arjunas.
And with a broad-headed arrow drawn back to his ear,
he severed from the body of the mighty Sudhanvan the head, which was radiant with the shimmering mass of light from its crown.
Having dispersed with the captivating wind-weapon (*pavanāstra*) the shower of weapons sent by him,
he made the earth invisible with heaps of those heads.
Pārtha brought about a terrible slaughter on the battlefield, destroying the Trigarta host by severing their umbrellas, banners, and chariots, and felling the arms and faces of the warriors.
***** The Battle with the Saṃśaptakas // 2 // ***** At this moment, when Droṇa had formed the Vainateya array,
the sons of Pāṇḍu advanced against the half-constructed array. Bhīṣma Parva 7.56.
Then, as the battle commenced and the destruction of the kings took place,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others fought against Droṇa and his chief followers.
When the sky was covered with dust and the quarters were blocked by arrows,
a terrible battle unfolded, indistinguishable and without bounds.
Then, as Droṇa was being assailed with the desire to capture the King of Dharma,
a terrible tumultuous roar arose from the troops for a moment.
Satyajit, whose valor is truth, approached to restrain that hero Kālāgnitejas, the foremost of all archers.
Then, having slain Vṛka, the prince, as he was fighting,
the preceptor covered Satyajit with arrows, making him like the sun whose rays are obscured.
Then, in a mere moment, Satyajit filled Droṇa with flaming arrows marked with the name "Hema," as if covering a tree with fireflies.
Then, with a broad-headed arrow, the Teacher struck off the head of the valiant Satyajit from his body— the head adorned with earrings that seemed to perform a fierce dance.
When Satyajit, the foremost of all archers,
had been struck down and the son of Dharma had fled, the army was utterly shattered.
***** The Slaying of Satyajit ***** Having slain Virāṭa’s younger brother Śatānīka, the striker Prahārin,
as well as Dṛḍhasena, Kṣatradeva, and King Vasudāna, [Arjuna departed]. (Bhagavadgītāmṛtavyākhyā 7.65)
Slaying the Cedis, Matsyas, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas with his golden chariot,
he fashioned a river for the garden of Death out of whirlpools of blood.
When the Pāṇḍava army had fled, being tormented by Droṇa’s arrows,
those led by Karṇa and Duryodhana honored the son of Bharadvāja.
When the army was rallied again by the mighty-armed Bhīma,
the assembled rulers of the earth rushed toward Droṇa in fury.
Bhīma was with horses the color of sages, Sātyaki with those possessing the luster of crystal,
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the commander of the army, with horses having the hue of pigeons.
Nakula and Sahadeva [rode] on horses with the luster of parrots and partridges; Abhimanyu on those with the hue of tawny deer; the Pāṇḍyas on those with the brilliance of snow;
and King Yudhiṣṭhira himself on steeds with the radiance of ivory and black manes.
Others, however, surrounding Droṇa in battle with various shadows of variegated armor, garments, and banners, made the world a realm consisting of arrows.
The two drums, Nandopanandaka, fashioned by divine machinery, served as the king’s banners; they shone resplendently for the one born of Dharma.
And the golden-bright images of Dharmarāja, Vāyu, Indra, and the Aśvins, as well as that of Draupadī’s son,
shone resplendent as they fought in the tumultuous fray.
Beholding Droṇa hemmed in by the kings with cruel intent,
the heroes Duryodhana and others rushed toward the warriors led by Bhīma.

While those foremost warriors, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, were engaged in single combats—those kings who delighted in the festival of battle—amidst those [weapons] of which arrows were the primary ones; Bhmj_7.75.
When Kṛtabāhu and Subāhu had been slain as heroes by Yuyutsu, and when the Vaṅga king, together with the Mātaṅgas, was struck down by Bhīmasena; ||| Bhmj_7.76 |||
When the Kaurava army had fled and the proud warriors were slain,
the worlds were shrouded in darkness by circles of the gloom of dust.
Urged on by Bhagadatta, Supratīka— resembling a cloud at the time of universal dissolution and overflowing with rut— plunged into the Pāṇḍava army.
Stationed in the abode of the Foe of Jambha to provide assistance in the battle against the Daityas,
the massing of Airāvaṇa’s herds was the very measure for his immense body.
Rising with his moon-white claws, he shone for a moment like Śeṣa when bitten by hundreds of snakes in their rage at being crushed by his own body.
"The source of all splendors, beginning with the moon and the sun"—
thus he was attended by garlands of constellations, like the mountain of sunrise.
"This army is in vain without the attainment of battle against the elephants of the quarters," as if saying this, the elephant, languid with rut, sighed with deep breaths.
"May these quarters come to their senses through the heat of my majesty"—
as if thinking thus, he fanned them again and again with his two ears like palm leaves.
With the sounds of the fierce ḍamaru drum of Caṇḍīśa and the resonance of loud ḍiṇḍima drums, he set forth,
his eyes slightly opening with effortless ease.
Having gone along, beholding at every step the earth strewn with the faces of heroes severed by the weapons of Bhagadatta, he remembered the lotus-pools.
Having entered the dense army of the Pāṇṍavas like an elephant,
he crushed the elephants and horses, creating a mire of fat and blood.
Being trampled by that lordly elephant, those armies of the enemies of the Kauravas suddenly recoiled, like prosperity shrinking away from pride.
As he was overwhelmed by that elephant, which was like Mount Mandara, the waves of his sword appeared like the Kalakuta poison rising from the ocean of the army.
With the tip of his trunk coiled into a ring, he rushed toward Vṛkodara;
people thought him to be drawn by one who held a noose in his hand.
Seeing Bhīma fallen into a state of peril, Yudhiṣṭhira quickly advanced against Bhagadatta together with all the lords of the earth.
Surrounded by those heroes, he slew the king of the Daśārṇas and,
with great force, overturned the chariot of Supratīka, O Sātyaki.
Then, by the elephant’s terrifying hissing sound accompanied by a spray of water,
the horses led by Bhīmasena were terrified and fled far away.
That army, oppressed by Bhagadatta mounted upon his elephant,
found no refuge anywhere, like a population under a cruel king.
As elephants were being struck down and chariots shattered, a tumultuous roar arose from the cries of "Alas! uttered by those filled with fear.
Hearing the cry of his own people, the son of Indra, having slain the Trigartas along with their followers by means of the Vajra weapon, then fell upon Bhagadatta.
Seeing the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow approaching swiftly like Tārkṣya,
the enraged lord of elephants was urged forward by Bhagadatta.
As he approached like the God of Death himself, Keśava,
by means of his chariot, rendered that futile assault to the right and once again took his place in front.
Having pierced Pārtha with a thousand arrows,
the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon, which Keśava then seized.
As Arjuna quickly protected himself, that weapon of the enemy of Kaiṭabha reached his chest and took on the splendor of a golden garland.
When that great weapon of blazing splendor had become fruitless,
Arjuna, out of embarrassment, spoke to Kṛṣṇa while twanging his bow.
"Surely I am unfit for battles, since you have taken up this weapon against me.
Hearing this, the one whose banner bears Garuḍa spoke to Pārtha, honoring him:
Previously, when Caturmūrti had died, this weapon of mine was bestowed upon Naraka, the son of the Earth, by me at the word of Pṛthivī.
Therefore, that lord of men obtained [the boon] from that Daitya not in vain;
I have now seized that divine [weapon], so let me slay this king.
When Janārdana had spoken thus, Savyasācin quickly covered Bhagadatta and his elephant with upward-pointing arrows.
Mounted upon his elephant on the peak of the mountain, the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa made the sky appear as if the celestial chariots of the immortals had been driven away not far off by his arrows.
Then, with a steel arrow drawn back to his ear and directed toward the tail, Pārtha pierced the lordly elephant between its temples, causing it great distress.
Pierced by Phalguna’s arrows, that lordly elephant-mountain struck down the army on the earth; for those who have fallen cause others to fall as well.
Then, enraged and pierced in the heart by Kirīṭin with a crescent-headed arrow,
Bhagadatta— having released his hook, bow, and arrows— became lifeless.
***** The Slaying of Bhagadatta // 4 // ***** When that hero, the preeminent among all kings, had fallen, the hope for victory in the Kuru army became slackened. Bhājya 7.109.
When the Kaurava army had fled, Vṛṣaka and Ācala, the two Gandhāra princes and sons of Subala,
both preeminent among archers, fought against Dhanañjaya.
Those two, who were raining down arrows, were struck together by a single shaft of Pārtha;
pierced through, they fell as if out of affection, having attained the state of *bhāruṇḍa* birds.
***** The Slaying of Vṛṣabha and Akaca ***** Seeing his two younger brothers slain, Śakuni trembled with rage;
conjuring vast illusions, he rushed toward Savyasācin. (Bhājana 7.112)
Surrounded on all sides by missiles, cruel beings, and darkness,
Pārtha did not tremble in battle, even before his hundreds of illusions.
Having severed that illusion which bewilders the timid with the Soura weapon, he dispatched Śakuni with another arrow; Śakuni then fled in fear.
Then, as the son of Subala thought this world belonged to Arjuna,
the Kuru army, fleeing in terror, found no refuge.
Then Droṇa, together with his armies and desiring to capture Yudhiṣṭhira,
rushed against the Pāñcālas, taking away the lives of the heroes.
As the armies were being slaughtered by the thousand by the one with the crimson horses,
the maiden Earth trembled as if intoxicated by the wine of blood.
"Strike Droṇa quickly! Protect him quickly in this battle!"—such was the great clamor that arose from both the Pāṇḍavas and their enemies.
Then, when the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas had been broken on all sides,
Nīla, the lord of Māhiṣmatī, fought against the Kuru army.
As he, possessing the brilliance of fire, scorched the ranks with divine weapons,
the archer Drauṇi alone, a treasury of fortitude, advanced against him.
Then the son of the Teacher, remaining unperturbed, severed the parasol, the banner, and the bow of him who was raining down adamantine arrows with his own broad-headed shafts.
Quickly alighting from his chariot, Nīla, of variegated prowess,
swooped down like a hawk with his sword to sever the head of the son of Droṇa.
The son of Bharadvāja, with a broad-headed arrow, struck off his lovely head, adorned with radiant earrings, like the moon joined by a pair of stars.
***** The Slaying of Nīla // 6 // ***** When Nīla had been killed and the circle of the Pāṇḍavas' great warriors was broken,
Pārtha, having slain the Saṃśaptakas, quickly returned to the field of battle. Bhmj_7.124 //
Then, as the enemy army was being broken by Bhīma, Phalguna, Saubhadra, Matsya, Caidya, and others, a tumultuous roar arose.
Then, a terrible clash occurred between those warriors skilled in combat, headed by Karṇa, which struck fear into all the worlds.
In that lawless battle, difficult to cross due to whirlpools of blood,
Karna, seeing the Kuru army shattered, fought against Pārtha.
With the fire-weapon (*pāvakāstra*), he made Arjuna and those led by Sātyaki appear like mountains turned tawny by a terrible conflagration of the quarters.
Then, led by Dhanañjaya, having destroyed that fierce array of weapons with their own weapons,
they made Karṇa resemble a dense forest of vetra-reeds with hundreds of arrows.
The one whose banner is the monkey dispatched Śatruñjaya, Vipāṭa, Vīra, Avaraja,
and Karṇānuja to the city of Yama with his arrows.
***** The Slaying of Karṇa’s Younger Brother // 7 // ***** Then all the great car-warriors of the Kauravas, led by Droṇa,
approached the side of Karṇa, unbearable with their blazing collections of weapons. Bhājya 7.131.
Those foremost of archers, engaged with Sātyaki and the others,
waged a terrible battle that caused the destruction of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, when those mighty-armed warriors were pierced by the torrent of Arjuna’s arrows,
the kings, severely afflicted, withdrew at the end of the day.
***** The Second Day of Battle // 8 // ***** Then,
having approached his preceptor at dawn, Duryodhana,
deeply distressed by the prowess of the Pāṇḍavas, spoke to him while making [him] hear [the situation]. (Bhagavadgītā 7.134)
"Alas! For me, who am devoid of merit, even you have promised [this hero];
yet this hero has come to fruitlessness for my grasping at the Dharma."
Those who are powerful, noble, and renowned do not learn in vain to fulfill the desires of those who love them— such as you are.
Having heard what was spoken by Suyodhana, the one born from a jar (Agastya) said:
"O King, the Pāṇḍava is difficult to capture, being protected by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow."
Nevertheless, today I shall do what is beneficial for you to the best of my ability;
let the Saṃśaptakas, however, go forth, having dragged Phalguna away from the battle.
When the Teacher had spoken thus, the hosts of Saṃśaptakas,
desiring to fight, challenged Arjuna once more and led him toward the southern direction.
Then Droṇa, the disciple of Rāma, consecrated for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas,
formed the Cakra-vyūha (the wheel-array), which is difficult to penetrate in the cycle of worldly existence.
In that city of ten thousand enemies,
ten thousand princes shone forth with arms adorned by banners as clear as the celestial river flowing through the sky.
"I do not consider King Suyodhana to be truly glorious,
for he stands there surrounded by a vast army of elephants and all the great chariot-warriors."
Accompanied by Jayadratha and the thirty younger brothers of Duryodhana, who were like the creators of the thirty gods, Droṇa took his position at the head of the battle formation.
Having seen that boundless force and the battle-array formed by those endowed with prowess,
the son of Dharma, whose army had been torn apart by Droṇa, fell into deep reflection.
Regarding Saubhadra in battle as being equal in prowess to the enemy of Kaṃsa and capable of conquering the three worlds, he spoke in the presence of the kings.
"Abhimanyu, your father has gone against the Saṃśaptakas;
therefore, you, who are even superior to him in virtue, must bear this burden."
"Whether it be Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, the son of Rukmiṇī, or you yourself whose prowess is like that of the wielder of the thunderbolt— the fifth capable of breaking the *cakravyūha* array does not exist."
Having heard this, the son of Subhadrā, his eyes wide with joy, said:
"By your command, I shall now enter, having shattered this military formation."
"Let the great chariot-warriors follow me,
who am unable to go forth," said the son of Arjuna to King Yudhiṣṭhira and the other monarchs.
When "So be it" was said, the son of Subhadrā urged the charioteer;
that hero, having cast off childhood, was like a three-year-old lion.
At the front of the battle, regarding all the kings as wretches,
he— beloved, clad in armor, with his limbs bound in mail, and adorned— [advanced].
Like a divine youth come to earth out of curiosity,
the hero possessed a form that was not at all harsh, yet he was a hero of mature prowess.
With his arrows, he made Droṇa’s army resemble the agitation of a turbulent ocean;
then the battle commenced, which bewildered even the great.
Having shattered the array, the son of Subhadrā, possessed of fierce prowess, entered; through his lightness, grace, and marvelous skill, he who was one became many.
Seeing that he had entered, all the Kuru heroes rushed toward him, crying out:
"He is captured! He has fled! He is slain! He is killing many!"
Thus arose the clamor of kings toward the chariot of Abhimanyu,
with heads still adorned with jeweled crowns and hands still grasping spears, swords, and arrows.
With bodies still clad in golden armor, with arms adorned with bracelets and armlets, with horses whose vital strength was severed, and with elephants whose frontal globes were shattered; Bhmj_7.157.
As he struck down the enemy without ceasing, he covered the earth with falling bodies; seeing his army being slaughtered by the striking son of Subhadrā, [the warriors fled].
Enraged, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the others rushed toward him;
having turned back those heroic showerers of arrows with their own shafts, they forced them to retreat.
Subhadrā’s son struck off the head of the King of Aśmaka with a broad-headed arrow;
then, when the Kuru army was broken, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa once again [attacked].
The son of Droṇa, the son of Hṛdika, the Gāndhāra, Śara, Śalya, Bṛhadbala,
Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, Citra, Duḥśāsana, and Suyodhana.
Other kings also approached and showered him with arrows;
by those swift, feathered shafts, the son of Arjuna was completely covered.
In the spring season, that beloved prince shone like a *karṇikāra* tree;
and the Dānavas were like [the attendants] of Kumāra to that son of Pṛthā.
In the battle, having been defeated by the power of the powerful one, they fled;
he, having slain the younger brother of the King of Madra, who possessed terrible prowess, quickly [proceeded].
Having defeated them one by one in succession, and having repeatedly overcome them when they were united, he slew Karṇa’s heroic brother, who roared like a thundercloud.
He brought about the destruction of kings headed by Karṇa and Duḥśāsana;
while he stood in the midst of the enemy forces, the rulers of the earth were present in all directions.
Due to his swiftness of hand, they beheld thousands of golden bows as he tore apart the host of elephants,
horses, and chariots with his feathered arrows.
Marked by chowries, turbans, and smiles, the river of blood flowed forth as headless trunks rose up and the circle of great warriors was broken.
The son of Pārtha blew his conch shell as if shattering the very quarters of the sky;
at that moment, the sons of Pāṇḍu were preparing to enter the battle array.
The arrogant King Jayadratha resisted Bhargava,
for he had previously been defeated by him at the hands of Maheśvara during the abduction of Kṛṣṇā.
The emaciated ascetic Phalguna obtained that victory without [the help of] Vara;
he shone forth, holding back the sons of Pandu along with their followers.
Like the shore-mountain [Velācala] bearing the surging waves of the great ocean,
he bore upon his banner a golden boar with the radiance of fire.
The ruler of the Sindhus scorched the Pāṇḍava army with the splendor of Rudra;
for when the sons of Pāṇḍu were forcibly held back by him alone, [the host was overwhelmed].
Entering among the kings, Abhimanyu cut down their heads like a forest;
that hero, having put Vṛṣasena, the son of Vaikartana, to flight.
In that tumultuous clash, when the quarters were obscured by dust, he carried off the head of the King of Kamboja, its turban disheveled.
The kings were made visible by the rays from their jewel-ornaments;
then the heir of victory, like a lion against a rutting elephant, [advanced].
When that best of kings, Abhimanyu, of incomparable splendor, had passed away, [the king] seized Satyaśravas.
Rukmaratha, the son of Śalya, rushed toward him while roaring;
he [was the target] of those whose mass of fire in the form of anger was visible through the smoke of their furrowed brows.
With the Gāndharva weapon, he suddenly reduced [his enemies] to mere remnants of fame;
by him, a hundred princes of similar age and appearance were slain.
When the forest of Rambhā’s thighs was shattered by him like a rutting elephant,
and the circle of kings had fled, Suyodhana’s pride was broken.
Then Duryodhana’s son Lakṣmaṇa, who was like Lakṣmaṇa himself, being pierced by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son, sighed deeply, bowed down with shame.
Approaching Abhimanyu, he discharged a volley of arrows,
like a cluster of young shoots upon the creeper of Fortune, into the cave of the tree of sensual enjoyment.
The son of Subhadrā fought that prince for a moment as an equal; his face was graced by rows of pearl necklaces like clusters of stars.

When the teacher had spoken thus, all the followers of Duryodhana stood firm in their resolve at the sacrifice of battle, where their very lives were the oblation.
Then, when the sun— the maker of day and possessor of the luster of a lotus— had set in the western quarter,
he was drawn away like a crimson parasol by the rafts of the evening's red rivers.
The vault of heaven was filled with stars trembling intensely, as if it were pervaded by the life-breaths of the kings slain in battle who were quivering with rage.
When the sky was shrouded in darkness by the solitary sword-forests,
it resembled the heavens being filled with celestial elephants who, though consumed by divine weapons, were destined for the third heaven.
With their crowns, armlets, golden arrows, and bows quivering,
those led by Duryodhana waged a terrible battle against their enemies.
The earth trembled from the thunderous roars of Arjuna’s chariot, the lion-like shouts of Māruti,
and the resounding twang of Droṇa’s bow.
As the Kuru and Pāṇḍava kings fought without ceasing,
the night shone forth like the Night of Doom (Kālarātri) herself arrived in person.
Darkness spread through the rhinoceroses and the elephants;
darkness—the state of poverty—spread through the parasols and the fans.
During that festival of the vultures, the earth became terrifying,
as if rent asunder by darkness through the absence of all measure.
The Vetālas, having been granted their fee,
became a festival of the grand spectacle of the dancing of their upraised, staff-like arms— headless trunks that abruptly shattered all composure.
The helmets, armor, falling weapons, and masses of flames shone like the tawny manes on the beards of the hordes of darkness-demons.
There, Droṇa, destroying the circle of kings with floods of great weapons,
severed the head of Śini, whose jeweled crown was ablaze.
Bhīmasena, having leaped from his chariot to the chariot of the powerful Kalinga prince, swiftly struck him down with his fist.
Struck by his fist in battle, his bones fell upon the ground like those of an old,
ripe tree struck down by the stones of Phalguna.
Having swiftly brought about the destruction of the Kalinga clan, Vṛkodara tore apart the two princes, Dhruva and Jaladhāra.
Having turned Karṇa’s younger brother, Duryodhana’s follower, away, the heroic Bhīma— difficult to overcome and invincible in his fury— struck him with his foot and crushed him.
Then Sātyaki, having slain Śala, the son of Somadatta, overwhelmed him—
who was already distressed by grief for his son— with arrows and turned him away from the fight.
As Sātyaki, showering volleys of arrows,
was tearing through the Kuru army and filling the quarters with his shafts, Aśvatthāman rushed toward him.
Seeing him destroying the ranks like another Rudra at midnight, Ghaṭotkaca rushed toward him with redoubled energy.
By his great roar, the quarters were completely filled;
whereupon they burst apart petal by petal, which was like a marvel.
In that battle, where Aśvatthāman was the source of radiance and Bāṇa the fierce-rayed sun,
Ghaṭotkaca shone forth, displaying the expansion of Rāhu’s yawn.
In that battle, the eyes of living beings could not endure the brilliance of the divine arrows released by the son of Droṇa, even though they were narrowed shut in the night.
Alone, the son of Droṇa fought against an akṣauhiṇī of Rākṣasas under the command of the son of Hiḍimbā, shattering their weapons as they attacked.
Having cut through the wheel, which was as radiant as the fire of time, Ghaṭotkaca joyfully struck his son, Añjanaparvan, who possessed terrible prowess.
Then, having severed the deluding illusion of the enraged Rākṣasa, the son of Droṇa slew Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s younger brothers in battle with his arrows.
Having slain thousands of the striking warriors of Kuntibhoja’s sons,
the son of Droṇa struck down the princes like the unrelenting God of Death.
In the meantime, Bhīmasena swiftly crushed the head of the lord of the Bāhlikas, who wore a crown, with his hero-slaying mace.
Then, filled with fury, he slew the ten younger brothers of Duryodhana:
Vīrabāhu, Dṛḍharatha, and Nāgadantamayaubhuja.
Having slain these seven Gandhāra princes— Pramāthin, Virajas, Suhasta, and likewise Sudṛḍha— he killed the sons of Subala.
Droṇa also fought with Yudhiṣṭhira himself in battle as he was slaughtering the Kaurava army,
employing the Aindra, Vāruṇa, and Vāyavya weapons.
Then, the son of Dharma, free from agitation, neutralized with his own Brahmā-weapon that Brahmā-weapon which had been discharged by his preceptor with the intent to seize him.
Seeing his army being trampled like a lotus pond by the sons of Pāṇḍu and their followers, who were like elephants, Suyodhana spoke to Karṇa.
Listen from ear to ear, O Karna, to the cries of the swift troops being slaughtered in battle by the victorious sons of Pāṇḍu.
O hero, as this tumultuous, lightless, and perilous situation has arisen, you alone are the refuge of splendors and our sole resort.
Thus requested by the king himself out of affection,
the son of Rādhā spoke to the Pāṇḍava armies, as if scattering volleys of arrows.
"O King, while Bhīṣma, the crest-jewel of all archers, lies upon his hero's bed, this burden has come to me by right of succession; why then do you speak thus? (Bhājana 7.590)
"Today, in this battle, I shall strike down with the Vāsavadattā spear even the diadem-wearing Arjuna, who has stripped Hara himself of his vow as a hero."
When the son of the Sūta had spoken thus, Kṛpa replied with a laugh:
"In this world, where the sons of Sūtas are not heroes, you alone have attained the status of a hero."
"Alas! O son of Rādhā, have your ears been rendered permanently deaf by all the heroes through this falsehood you have spoken? (Bhājana 7.593)
"O valiant one, why have you arrived here as if unaware of the news?
When the Lord of Sindhu was slain, did you not act then?"
We have all seen the essential strength of both you and the son of Pāṇḍu;
fight according to your actual power, but do not indulge in vain boasting.
When Śāradvata had spoken thus, Vaikartana said in anger:
"Heroes roar fruitfully, like clouds in the rainy season."
But you, an old man devoid of proper conduct, speak thus out of sheer delusion;
for who, unless he has taken the side of another, would praise others like a hired bard?
"O wretched Brahmin, if you speak thus again out of hatred, I shall cut off your bitter tongue with this very sword."
Seeing his maternal uncle thus provoked to fury by Karṇa,
the son of Droṇa drew his sword and rushed at him in a rage.
As he approached, equal to Rudra and capable of bringing about the dissolution of the three worlds,
the king himself restrained him and Gautama with words of prudent counsel.
Then, having propitiated Droṇa and Karṇa,
he, intent on battle, entered the Pāṇḍava army along with all the great chariot-warriors.
Likewise, by the ear-piercing arrows released from his bow drawn back to his ear,
Yudhiṣṭhira’s army was scattered in every direction.
Approaching that fierce fire of Karṇa, which was as formidable as a forest conflagration at the end of autumn,
the cloud that was Pārtha covered it with showers of arrows.
Then, in an instant, his bow, chariot, and banner shattered by Arjuna's arrows,
Karna— his hopes destroyed— climbed onto the chariot of Kṛpa.
Seeing the hero Duryodhana fighting with his enemies, the son of Droṇa,
who was difficult to overcome in battle, slaughtered the Pāñcāla army.
Being slaughtered by the thousands by the son of Droṇa— that fire to the forest of the kṣatriyas— the surviving Pāñcālas fled in all directions.
Then, having defeated the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna and slain his followers,
the son of Droṇa turned the battlefield into a garden of Death.
King Yudhiṣṭhira himself, accompanied by Bhīma and Arjuna,
having put the Kaurava army to flight, left only Droṇa remaining.
Then Sātyaki, unperturbed, fought like Kumāra against Tāraka, as Somadatta of vast prowess advanced against him.
Pierced by those hundreds of arrows, Sātyaki suppressed his pain and,
tearing him apart with a thunderbolt-like shaft, felled him to the ground.
Then, in that battle between Droṇa and Arjuna, which was difficult to endure due to the multitude of divine weapons,
the night shone like the Night of Doom (Kālarātrī) clothed in red garments.
Then, led by Kirīṭin and dispatched by Droṇa and Kṛpa,
there arose a terrifying roar from the breaking ranks of the armies.
Then, by the command of Duryodhana, the heroes fought in dense darkness with lamps continuously strung together, which were attached to elephants and horses.
In an instant, those two armies shone all around with heaps of lamps,
as if with the splendors of slain kings that had been reduced to fragments.
Those armies shone with the reflections of lamps upon their swords,
like forests ablaze at night with circles of medicinal herbs.
The radiance of the jewel-ornaments of the lords of men, illuminated by lamps,
shone like streaks of gold upon a touchstone for darkness.
Then, when those lamps had been extinguished in that conflict,
midnight attained its prime, as enmities do through stratagems.
Then, when that battle characterized by heroism had proceeded without distinction,
the Lord of the Kauravas, along with his followers, was himself conquered by the son of Dharma.
Even when Sahadeva had reached the path of death,
Karṇa did not slay him in battle, for he repeatedly remembered the words of Kuntī.
Then the heroic Vṛṣasena, son of Karṇa, entered the enemy host,
his forest of Kṣatriyas being licked by the flames of his multitude of weapons.
When the heroes had been put to flight by Vṛṣasena’s arrows,
the son of Draupadī, enraged with fury, began to tear through the Kuru army.
While that terrible battle was raging and while the son of Bharadvāja looked on,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna slew the heroic king Drumasena.
Then, at the word of Duryodhana, Droṇa and Karṇa created,
as it were, lotus-pools upon the earth with the severed heads of the kings.
Having defeated those led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and destroyed the leaders of the opposing forces,
Karṇa put the Pāṇḍava army to flight and caused a slaughter of kings.
The enemies could not bear to look upon that Karṇa, a treasury of splendor born of the Sun, as he scattered his arrows in battle.
As the armies were being broken by Karṇa, who was preeminent in battle,
the entire hope for victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu diminished.
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, Ghaṭotkaca swiftly slew Karṇa during the night, like the wrath of Kṛṣṇa falling upon him.
When he had risen, with his blazing beard, tongue, and eyes,
the armies fled in a hundred directions as if struck down by his majesty.
Then Pārtha, with the dark luster of a rain cloud, his knitted brows like fierce lightning, overwhelmed Karṇa with hundreds of wide-spreading showers.
He stood upon a chariot four hundred cubits long, its body like molten gold,
capable of rivaling a blue mountain from which fire blazes in every direction.
Holding a radiant bow ten cubits in circumference,
like fire consuming a great sāl tree set ablaze by a forest conflagration.
With his broad crown shimmering and his armlets of blazing Jāmbūnada gold,
he shone as if ready to shatter the peaks of the mountain of darkness.
His loud laughter was like the roar of the darkness;
seeing that fierce flame, there arose the cry of pain from those who were torn asunder.
When the enemy armies had fled and the kings were fit for enjoyment,
the mountain that was the son of Rādhā alone swallowed up his storm of arrows.
Then, for the protection of the King of Aṅga, the powerful Alambuṣa, son of Jaṭāsura,
took leave of the Lord of the Kauravas and advanced.
Then there occurred a terrible battle between him and the striker Ghaṭotkaca, who rained down weapons, missiles, stones, and fire.
As those two fought, manifesting wonderful peaks of illusion,
hundreds of their warriors met their destruction through the powerful roars [of the other].
Then, having rushed from his chariot to the other chariot,
the son of Bhīma embraced Alambuṣa with both arms like a friend and squeezed him very tightly.
As he was being squeezed, jets of blood issued forth from the openings of his channels,
accompanied by smoke, flames of fire, and a loud sound.
Then, having crushed that screaming one upon the ground, Ghaṭotkaca violently tore off his head and rushed toward Duryodhana.
He said to him: "O lowest of kings, this kinsman of yours, a night-stalker, has been slain by me; now strike off the head of your beloved once again."
Having said this, the night-stalker rushed toward Karṇa,
roaring like the turbulent Time itself, driven by a fierce wind.

***** The Slaying of Alambusa // 22 // ***** Then, as the terrible battle between the son of Rādhā and the Rākṣasa proceeded, the gods in heaven remembered the conflict between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. Bhmj_7.643 //
Though pierced by the Rākṣasa with arrows as thick as pillars, which were like blazing torches,
the high-minded Karṇa did not waver.
Then, pierced by broad ear-arrows discharged by those free from anger,
the Rākṣasa hurled a discus toward Karṇa’s ear.
Beholding that discus with its thousand spokes, which was turning the sky tawny with its brilliance, Karṇa furiously shattered it into pieces with his swift arrows.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, out of anger, having employed a deluding illusion,
crushed the chariot of the Sūta’s son and entered the vast sky.
In that cremation ground, which consists of a fire of peaceful splendor and is strewn with stars and bones, there are tens of millions of intoxicated vetālas serving as her seat.
Now an elephant, now a lion, for a moment a cloud, and for a moment a mountain—
possessing a massive body composed of all living beings, he rained down vast boulders.
Discharging fire from the earth, weapons from heaven, and a circle of Rākṣasas from all directions upon the Kuru armies, he fought against the son of Vikartana.
Then, having dispelled that illusion by the power of his divine weapons, Karṇa,
scorching the Pāṇḍava army, pierced the Rākṣasa with his arrows.
Slaying thousands of Yātudhānas,
Karṇa, the foremost of archers, shone with the prowess of Rāma.
The son of Bhīma discharged at Karṇa a thunderbolt fashioned by Rudra himself, which possessed sixty-four wheels and was terrifying with its tongue of Time.
Released by the lord of the Rākṣasas, that weapon of great roar, capable of crushing masses of mountains,
reduced the chariot of the son of Adhiratha to ashes.
Then, mounting another chariot, the son of the charioteer struck down other flesh-eaters who had the faces of piśācas.
Deprived of his chariot, Ghaṭotkaca, a master of great illusions, whose eyes were encircled by the flames of the fire of his wrath, vanished once again.
In the meantime, Baka’s dear friend Alāyudha, the lord of the Rākṣasas, being permitted by Suyodhana, approached Bhīma.
He stood upon a chariot of deep resonance, yoked to a hundred horses that had the ears of elephants and the luster of the faces of *piśācas*.
Bhīma received him, who roared with a heavy and furious rage,
as an unshakable hero receives a risen *vetāla* when a mantra has been perfected.
Being assailed by the terrible Rākṣasa, who rained down a shower of stones and weapons,
Bhīma hurled his mace with the intent to slay him.
Having struck that mace, adorned with golden armlets, with his own mace,
the Rākṣasa entered the sky, roaring with a voice as deep as the rumbling of the clouds at the end of time.
Seeing Bhīma engaged in combat at night with Alāyudha, who fought with deceitful tactics, Kṛṣṇa became momentarily overwhelmed with doubt.
Then, at the word of Śauri, the hero Ghaṭotkaca, the foremost among those of fierce deeds,
abandoned Karṇa and rushed toward Alāyudha.
As those two raged in the sky, their collision produced a sound like a thundercloud,
fiercely emitting fire from the friction of their stones and weapons.
From those two, whose beards and matted locks were tawny like funeral pyres and who were terrifying to behold,
sparks seemed to fly about as they were produced by the clashing of their teeth.
Ghaṭotkaca swiftly severed the head of Alāyudha, which was adorned with two earrings resembling fire-pits.
***** The Slaying of Alāyudha // 23 // Having slain him, the son of Hiḍimbā, of terrible prowess,
let out a fierce roar and, quickly approaching Karṇa, struck him with showers of stones. Bhājya 7.667.
Vaikartana, having decimated the army of the Pārthas,
became agitated by Ghaṭotkaca and filled him with nets of arrows.
Then, having destroyed Karna’s chariot with the Astra weapon,
the night-stalker assumed a delusion that bewilders the three worlds and entered the sky.
With firebrands as weapons, with trees, stones, and likewise with mountains,
he of the great roar struck down the army of the Kauravas.
At midnight, while all the heroes were engaged in combat with the Rākṣasa,
the protectors of the earth fled, their chariots and elephants shattered.
During that most terrifying slaughter of all the warriors,
Karṇa remained unshaken in battle and filled the sky with his arrows.
As the arrows pierced the rocks suspended in the sky,
which were matted with masses of flames, there arose a crackling sound.
Then there were iron clubs, swords, *śataghnīs*, spears, and mallets;
as well as tridents, maces, discs, *bhuśuṇḍis*, arrows, and javelins.
By that Rākṣasa, a fierce warrior who cast [his weapons] into Karna’s face,
the Kaurava army was made to appear as if slaughtered by hundreds of Deaths.
And while the army was thus fleeing, descending into rivers of blood,
and while the son of Rādhā remained steadfast despite being without support, [the earth shook].
When the Siddhas and celestial rishis had departed through the sky after saying "May it be well," the entire world trembled due to the illusory power of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Then, approaching the hero Karṇa as he was fighting, the Kaurava spoke,
distressed by the exhaustion and terror of the universal slaughter.
"Why do you carry this spear for the sake of slaying Arjuna?
For who among us could escape from him at such a midnight hour, were he even to conquer him?"
Having heard this, Rādheya [reflected upon] that weapon of great splendor given by Śakra,
which had been preserved for a very long time for the sake of slaying the sole hero.
He discharged the *dāraṇī* [missile] that rends the hosts of Daityas into the expanse of the sky,
by the splendor of whose garland of flames the atmosphere became as if marked with a parting line.
Having rent asunder the firm chest of the radiant rākṣasa, she,
blazing like another power of life, ascended to the third heaven.
Then the son of Hiḍimbā, who resembled Mount Mandara, being consumed by fire,
fell with his heart pierced, crushing the Kuru army as he descended.
***** The Slaying of Ghaṭotkaca in the Night Battle // 24 // ***** When the heroic Ghaṭotkaca, who possessed the prowess of the Ten-Necked One (Rāvaṇa), was slain,
the Kurus were overjoyed and honored Karṇa, who was like Rāma.
Then, as Karṇa was rendered powerless, the slayer of Kāliya,
Viṣṇu, danced within the Pāṇḍava army, overflowing with joy.
As he danced, his arms, clad in fluttering yellow garments,
shone like trees with swaying clusters of blossoming filaments shaken by the wind.
Afflicted by the grief of Haiḍimba’s slaughter, Pārtha spoke to him in reproach:
"O Janārdana, what is this joy of yours at a time of despair?"
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa said: "Friend, Karṇa is now defeated;
the life-force of the son of Hiḍimbā has become as fickle as a thought."
And the power from Karṇa’s staff-like arms has gone forth together with you for victory;
likewise, Ekalavya, Jarāsaṃdha, Śiśupāla, and others have been dealt with by me.
"Having known this battle beforehand, those who were difficult to conquer were slain by my powers;
in this very same way, Karṇa cannot be defeated in combat even by the thirty gods."

How much more so, O Pārtha, with that terrible spear given by Vāsava; why did he not hurl that spear at you, though he was constantly deluded by me and urged every night by the wicked Kauravas, O Karṇa? (Bhājana 7.691)
When the descendant of Daśārha had spoken thus, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, afflicted by the slaughter of their heroic Siddhas and blinded by rage, fought without distinction.
When the son of Hiḍimbā was slain, King Yudhiṣṭhira, tormented by grief,
was consoled by Keśava and, filled with wrath, rushed toward Karṇa.
Followed by all the kings, he entered the Kuru army;
having approached, the venerable Vyāsa addressed Dharmarāja.
"By good fortune, O hero, the world has not been rendered devoid of Arjuna by the spear of Adhiratha’s son; now fight without agitation and free from haste."
"In four days from now, the rulers of the earth shall no longer exist.
O hero of Dharma, abandon your anger; victory always belongs to those who follow the Dharma. (Bhājana-vyākaraṇa 7.696)
When Vyāsa had vanished after saying this, Bhīma, Arjuna,
and Yudhiṣṭhira engaged in a terrible battle with Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the others.
That night was a dark night for heroes, a festival for yakṣas and rākṣasas,
and it became a night of three watches for the kings.

Then, seeing the army overcome by sleep and stilled after being wounded by weapons, Śvetāśva, a treasury of glory, spoke out of compassion: Bhājana-varga 7.699: tato nidrākule sainye śānte śastrakṛtakṣate / dṛṣṭvā jagāda kāruṇyācchvetāśvo yaśasāṃ nidhiḥ // 699 //
In this lightless moment, let all these great chariot-warriors, being weary,
enjoy rest for a while with their eyes closed in sleep.
When this was said, all the soldiers, praising Dhanañjaya,
abandoned their fatigue for a moment while seated upon the backs of elephants and the seats of chariots.
With their elephants and horses motionless, their parasols and fly-whisks still,
and their soldiers with weapons resting upon their shoulders, those armies became as if fixed in place.

Then the moon rose, possessing the beauty of a jeweled mirror for the adornment of the women that are the quarters of the sky; it was like a sword-blade for the firmament, a conch-shell for the tusks of the world-elephant, and a swan upon the river of its own radiance.
Then, with the glories of all the heroes who fell in the face-to-face battle,
he filled the sky as the moon fills it with its rays.
For a moment, they shone like kings being fanned by fly-whisks, as they were fanned by the nectar-rayed moon’s beams, which were as beautiful as frost-dispelling fire.
The moon sprouted upon the arrows, its foliage grew thick upon the waves,
it blossomed upon the tigers of the kings, and it bore fruit within their conch shells.
The moon, reflected in the red rivers,
shone with a reddish luster as if reeling from the intoxication of twilight.
Then, when the night had waned like the wasting disease of consumption,
the blessed Lord of Day rose, copper-red with blood.

***** On the fourth day, there was a night battle. // 25 // Tormented by the words of Duryodhana, the Pot-born [Agastya] then, in his wrath, consumed even those unacquainted with divine weapons with celestial missiles. Bhmj_7.709 //
When the battle resumed again, lawless and bringing about the destruction of the world,
a tumultuous roar of joy arose among those being slain by Droṇa.
At that time, when the end of the eon was not yet due, the sky-dwellers said: "Has Rudra, with this form of his, prepared to annihilate the worlds?"
The Cedis, Somakas, Pañcālas, Matsyas, Kekayas, and Sṛñjayas—
those heroes, oppressed by Droṇa’s arrows, found no peace.
Then Virāṭa and Drupada, having covered the son of Bharadvāja with sharp arrows,
quickly caused amazement among your archers.
Then Droṇa, having slain the sons of Pārṣata who possessed great prowess,
simultaneously severed the necks of Virāṭa and Drupada with two broad-headed arrows.
***** The Slaying of Virāṭa and Drupada // 26 // ***** When the armies of the Matsyas and Pañcālas had been broken, the son of the Wind-god (Bhīma),
together with Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others, rushed against Droṇa’s division. Bhmj_7.715 //
Then Karna, Saubala, Hārdikya, Duḥśāsana, and others fought against Bhīma, Pārṣata, Saineya, Phalguna, and the rest.
In that tumultuous, violent clash of all the heroes,
there arose a river garlanded with surging waves, its branching streams being the disheveled locks of hair.

Seeing Droṇa causing a slaughter of the Pāñcālas, Cedis, and Matsyas in battle, the enemy of Kaṃsa (Kṛṣṇa) spoke to the son of Pāṇḍu (Arjuna): Bhājya 7.718: Seeing Droṇa causing a slaughter of the Pāñcālas, Cedis, and Matsyas in battle, the enemy of Kaṃsa (Kṛṣṇa) spoke to the son of Pāṇḍu (Arjuna).
This disciple of Jamadagnya has grown into a fire for the kṣatriyas;
with its unbearable flames of divine weapons, by whom among us can it be endured?
Fighting with his full might, armed and formidable, my preceptor is prepared this very day to make the world devoid of Pāṇḍavas; so I know.
"Having heard that his son has been slain, he will certainly not fight;
therefore, relying on a stratagem, let a policy be devised for victory."
Having heard this, King Arjuna, the lord of the Pāṇḍavas, covered his ears and stood with his face cast down; somehow, he remained silent, having reluctantly accepted the situation.
Having struck down his intoxicated elephant named Aśvatthāman with his mace,
Bhīma loudly announced the death of his son to Droṇa in his presence.
Out of shame, Bhīma spoke very unpleasant words;
yet Droṇa, considering his son to be invincible, did not believe it to be so.
Having entered the Pāñcāla ranks with the intent to slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
he then destroyed sixty thousand chariots of heroic warriors.
With fierce prowess, the enraged Droṇa, like a second Rudra, consumed millions of the Cedis, Pañcālas, and Matsyas with the Brahmāstra.
Slaying the heroic Prabhadrakas and the striking Somakas,
he moved about with the pride of a youth of four hundred years.
Then the sages, having approached him who had committed such a most cruel deed,
restrained him from that terrible slaughter which would have brought about the destruction of the world.
When the assembly of sages had departed through the sky, Droṇa, remembering the words of Bhīma,
questioned Yudhiṣṭhira— whose prowess is truth— with a mind filled with apprehension.
Requested with effort by Govinda for the sake of pacifying the destruction of the world,
Yudhiṣṭhira, having said that very thing, spoke freely of the elephant.
The horses carried Yudhiṣṭhira without touching the ground;
yet, by moving so low, they quickly became as if heavy with falsehood.
Then, as if his vital organs had been pierced by poisoned iron arrows,
Droṇa, having resolved upon his own death, became like one depicted in a painting.
To him, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, whose arrows were like flames upon his tongue, quickly said:
"Aha! Having become a Brahmin in body, you are pitiless like a flesh-eater;
even though your own dear son has been slain, you perform such a foul deed!"
Having heard that, Droṇa suddenly cast aside his bow in a fit of rage;
having granted safety to all, he became silent and beheld an inner light.
From the falling away of the three pairs of that aggregate of six sheaths,
the light emerged from the aperture of Brahmā and entered the void.
In the meantime, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, blinded by rage, violently pulled him by the hair, even as he was being restrained with urgency by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
While his teacher’s weapon was not yet drawn, and while his splendor had already transferred to [his own] body,
he struck off the head with a sword, though reproached by the lords of the rivers.
***** The Slaying of Droṇa // 27 // ***** When the hero on the golden chariot, the preceptor of all archers, was slain,
all the great car-warriors of the Kauravas fled in utter confusion. Bhājana 7.738.
Seeing the Kuru army broken, the son of Droṇa became apprehensive and,
with tearful eyes, asked Suyodhana, "What is this?"
While he was hanging head-downwards, unable to speak out due to his agony,
Gautama, impelled by him, announced the murder of his father.
Having heard of that terrible slaughter perpetrated through deceit against his preceptor by the cruel Pāñcālya, he blazed with the fire of wrath.
As he sighed in anger, like Time itself desiring to consume all things,
a state of agitation arose among all beings that was exceedingly terrifying.
Pressing his hand against his hand, he said with tearful eyes:
"Alas! Even my father has suffered the seizing of his hair!"
Having caused his preceptor to be slain through falsehood, how can that king who acts like a crane obtain the earth while I am still alive, O son of Kuntī? (Bhagavad Gītā 18.744)
Today, when the son of Pāṇḍu along with all the kings has been consumed by my wrath,
the heroes of the Kṣatriya clans will remember Bhārgava, the destroyer of their race.
Having today made the son of Pṛṣata a sacrificial animal as an offering for the fire of my wrath,
I am now prepared to rid the earth of those who are not Kṛṣṇa’s allies.
Long ago, my father bestowed upon me this weapon spoken by Nārāyaṇa;
let the sky-dwellers behold today the worlds destroyed by me with it.
Having spoken thus, he— self-controlled and pure— aimed that blazing weapon,
by which the three worlds trembled like trembling leaves of the holy fig tree.
Then the son of Droṇa let out a roar like the sound of the ocean agitated by Mount Mantha,
by which all the directions seemed to be shattered to pieces.
Then, beholding his own army distressed, Śvetavāhana,
gasping and overwhelmed with remorse, said to the son of Dharma:
"A teacher has been slain by a disciple who, greedy for wealth, acted under a pretext."
While the son of the king of the gods was thus loud-mouthed with idle chatter, the son of the Wind-god, his eyes copper-red with anger toward his preceptor, spoke.
O Pārtha, you ought not speak like a sage;
for who would overlook the rules of conduct toward an enemy in battle who has committed a terrible injury?
While this heroic arm of mine, so fond of the mace, stands here,
and you, O Kṛṣṇa, are present, why indeed is the praise of Droṇa’s son being celebrated?
When Bhīmasena had spoken thus, Pārṣata said to Arjuna:
"This kinsman of Brahmins, who stood engaged in improper acts and was a destroyer of the worlds, has been slain by me."
He by whom even an ordinary man like Muktavarman was slain with the Brahmāstra—
that thorn in the side of the world must be destroyed by every possible means, like an asura.
"How was Bhīṣma slain by you, as well as that lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, the friend of your father? What of this? The deeds of heroes are indeed profound."
Having heard Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s words, Arjuna, his eyes turned askance and squinting, sighed, tormented by anger, and cried out, "Fie! Fie! (Bhājana 7.757).
When the son of Dharma had bowed in shame and the kings had become silent,
Sātyaki, burning with anger, addressed Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Alas, we are all indeed wicked, we who address as if with greetings one who stands before us having slain his guru; you must be slain with every effort!
When the son of Śini had spoken thus, the son of Drupada said:
"Aha! You who know the faults of others speak as if you were yourself faultless."
Bhūriśravas, who had gone to the fast unto death with his arm severed by Kirīṭin—
by what other cruel man of fallen conduct was he struck down?
"You must not speak thus to the king; otherwise, with sharp arrows, I shall bring you back to humility through my teachers of discipline."
As they spoke thus and were impetuously intent on slaying one another,
Bhīmasena, along with his younger brothers, restrained them by the word of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, in an instant, when the ocean-like army of the Kuru king had returned,
the ten directions could no longer be discerned, being shrouded by the weapons of Droṇa’s son.
Being struck by the blazing circles of weapons discharged from the Nārāyaṇa-weapon,
the army of the Pāṇḍavas was reduced to a mere remnant.
In that terrible slaughter of great warriors, which was filled with hundreds of flames born from the clashing of weapons,
King Yudhiṣṭhira was terrified.
Looking toward the son of Pṛṣata and at Kirīṭin, he said:
"Let everyone flee from here; a great danger has arrived."
The victorious one, though established in neutrality, was provoked to anger by the death of his preceptor—
that aged man by whom the boy Abhimanyu was treacherously struck down.
By him those great chariot-warriors, headed by Satyajit, were slain;
he who gave to Duryodhana an invulnerable, divine armor.
"Let no more fighting be done now; may it be well with the wise son of Pṛthā.
Thus shall I enter the fire; who could withstand the son of Droṇa, who is like Death itself?"
When this was said by Dharmarāja, Keśava raised his arms and spoke loudly to the kings, who were blazing with the splendor of their weapons:
"O you all, cast away your weapons and descend from your chariots to the ground!
By this weapon, those who are weaponless and standing on the earth are slain."
While the enemy of Kaiṭabha was speaking thus with agitation and vehemence, Bhīma addressed the kings: "You ought to grant me freedom from fear."
"Here I am, clad in armor and having taken up my mace which proclaims the covenant;
I am prepared to slay the son of Droṇa—let the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas behold me! (Bhājana 7.774)
As the son of Droṇa approached, roaring thus,
he laughed and said, "This one is a fool," and covered him with a multitude of arrows.
Then, being scorched on all sides by the Nārāyaṇa weapon,
the kings cast aside their weapons and descended from their mounts to the ground.
As Bhīmasena stood upon his chariot and fought without agitation,
a circle of weapon-flames fell upon him, merging into one.
Seeing Bhīma momentarily obscured by the collision of the peaks of the swift flames of fire,
Arjuna discharged the Varuṇa weapon.
Struck on all sides by the fiery flames of the Nārāyaṇa weapon, that [opposing] weapon was rendered futile in an instant, as if it had never been discharged at all in the sky.
As Vṛkodara stood in the midst of that terrible and great danger from weapons,
the two Kṛṣṇas quickly descended from their chariot and dragged him away by his arms.
Having forcibly seized the weapon and quickly brought the hero down from his chariot to the ground,
the two heroes Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava stood there, joyful and resplendent with their diverse splendor.
Then, when that weapon had been pacified by itself and the three worlds were restored to peace,
Duryodhana said to the son of Droṇa, "Let another weapon be employed."
Saying, "A divine weapon must not be used twice," the son of Droṇa, though agitated,
brought about the destruction of the Pañcālas, Matsyas, and Kekayas with his arrows.
Having defeated Sātyaki and the son of Pṛṣata, and having put the army to flight,
he slew the hero Paurava and King Sudarśana.
When the Pāṇḍava armies had been broken and were fleeing after the son of Droṇa,
Dhanañjaya himself, filled with wrath, checked him with showers of arrows.
Then, for the destruction of the worlds, the son of Droṇa raised the terrible fire-weapon (āgneya-astra), which enveloped the sky with a garland of flames.
Then all those best of kings, as if completely covered in golden armor and pervaded by the splendor of great weapons, fell to the ground.
Seeing the Akṣauhiṇī army consumed by the weapon and enveloped in flames, Dhanañjaya manifested the fierce Brahmāstra to quell it.
When that weapon had vanished and Keśava and Arjuna were liberated, the son of Droṇa, seeing this, became enraged and exclaimed, "Fie upon weapons! (Bhājana 7.789).

In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa— the sage who possesses a thousand rays of wisdom, who is a bridge across the shoreless ocean of the nectar of the Vedas, and who is a royal swan upon the Mānasa lake of Sarasvatī— though dark, appeared as if not dark at all.
Abandoning that chariot, the son of the Preceptor, a man of fierce deeds, bowed down and asked:
"O Blessed One, why have your divine weapons become fruitless against Pārtha accompanied by Kṛṣṇa?"
Thus questioned by one agitated with anger, the lord of sages said to him:
"These two heroes, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, are the ṛṣis Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
In ancient times, Nārāyaṇa, having performed austerities for sixty thousand years and having propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow, attained equality with him.
This very Kṛṣṇa, O son of Droṇa, is himself difficult to conquer and is personally devoted to the vow of worshipping the Liṅga;
you too are a portion of Rudra, therefore do not fall into agitation.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the son of the Guru, his anger subsided;
having mentally paid homage to Rudra, he disregarded the two divine Kṛṣṇas.
Then, when the withdrawal of the armies had been ordered by the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
Pārtha returned from the battle and beheld Vyāsa on the road.
Having paid homage to him, he asked: "O Blessed One, previously in battle, I saw a man with a spear in his hand, possessing the brilliance of fire."
I saw the army of Kuru being consumed on all sides by countless, blazing circles of tridents that had issued forth from that trident-wielder.
"Having touched the earth for half a *krośa*, fierce like another Rudra, he was questioned by Dhanañjaya; thus spoke the delighted Dvaipāyana. (Bhāj 7.799)
That god is the enemy of Tripura, the crusher of the demon Gajāsura,
Rudra, the fire that is the end-maker, and one capable of bringing about the dissolution of the three worlds.
Having paid homage to that giver of boons, by whom the deities in heaven shine,
he of the smiling countenance paralyzed the pillar-like arm of the enemy of Jambha.
Meditate upon that Hara, the destroyer of Smara and the enemy of the Asuras, who possesses a smiling radiance; who is ageless, invincible, eternal, and the universal form;
who is the unequal-eyed, the masterless, the peaceful, the lord of Uma, the Sovereign, whose mass of splendor is as vast as a garland of the most youthful suns.

I bow to Śiva— the destroyer of the eye of the Sun (Rudra), the obstructer of Dakṣa’s consecration, who is both existence and non-existence, without duality, perceivable through a pure state of being,
auspicious, immovable, inconceivable, adorned with the crescent moon, and the most eminent in the gambling assembly with the daughter of the Mountain Lord.
After the son of Indra had expressed his supreme insistence on the matter of the slaughter and departed for the crest-jewel of sages out of affection,
the kings entered their camps at the close of day and held conversations centered upon the exploits of preeminent heroes.
Thus ends the Droṇaparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
